c.tagline: The 'Pearl of the South', Paraguay's river-beach and Carnival capital.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis are largely unmetered, so agree the fare before setting off; the local MUV app (and limited Uber) give upfront prices, and city buses are the budget option.

emergency.note: 911 is Paraguay's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets in the Carnaval crowds and along the busy costanera on summer nights.

hood_desc: The downtown core around the Cathedral and the main commercial streets, rebuilt into a modern grid of wide avenues after the Yacyretá dam flooded the old 'Zona Baja'; best for first-timers wanting shops, markets and services within walking distance.

The waterfront tourist zone on the Costanera with San José Beach, Paraguay's most popular river beach, backed by restaurants, bars and the Sambadrome that hosts the Encarnaceno Carnival; the liveliest and most convenient base for visitors.
A calm residential neighbourhood of leafy streets and family homes set back from the river; suits travellers wanting a quiet, local base near the centre.
A largely residential and commercial district near the bus terminal and main access roads; a practical, quiet base for onward travel to Asunción or the Jesuit ruins.
A newer beach and residential area to the west along the Costanera with Chaipé Beach and open riverside space; suits travellers wanting quieter sands away from the main crowds.
lodging: De la Trinidad Hotel Casino Resort

water.note: City tap water is treated, but most visitors stick to bottled.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 05:00 to around 22:30; taxis and ride apps fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Encarnación has no metro or tram; the city runs on local buses, taxis and ride apps like MUV, with a very walkable Costanera waterfront and downtown.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (guaraníes) to the driver; there is no smartcard system.

air: Teniente Amín Ayub González Airport (ENO) — limited regional flights
Libertador General José de San Martín Airport (PSS), Posadas, Argentina — nearest full-service airport
Silvio Pettirossi International Airport (ASU), Asunción — main international gateway
bus: International buses across the San Roque González bridge to Posadas, Argentina
Long-distance coaches to Asunción and Ciudad del Este
train: Posadas–Encarnación International Train (cross-border shuttle over the bridge)

tip.r: Tipping is not obligatory; rounding up or leaving around 10% at restaurants for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Chipa
food.desc: Ring of cassava-starch bread bound with cheese, egg and pork fat, best eaten still hot; vendors work the streets and buses from dawn.

places.name: Chipa Tia
places.note: Chipa specialist with everything from plain rings to ham-and-cheese versions.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Bakers sell them straight from the tatakua clay oven each morning.

places.name: Terminal de Omnibus vendors
places.note: Basket sellers board the buses; the classic way Paraguayans buy chipa.

food.name: Sopa paraguaya
food.desc: Not a soup at all: a dense, savoury cornbread rich with cheese, onion and milk, cut in squares beside grilled meat.

places.name: El Quincho
places.note: Central restaurant known for Paraguayan classics served with the asado.

places.name: Parrillada Don Emilio
places.note: Grill house where sopa paraguaya is the standard side to the meat.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Sold by the slab at market kitchens for a fraction of restaurant prices.

food.name: Mbeju
food.desc: Flat starch-and-cheese griddle cake, crisp outside and stretchy inside, traditionally eaten with tereré on cold mornings.

places.name: Taberna La Cava
places.note: Serves mbeju and bori bori among its Paraguayan plates in a relaxed cellar setting.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Cooked to order on flat pans at the market food stalls.

places.name: Costanera food kiosks
places.note: Riverfront stands sell mbeju and chipa to walkers along the promenade.

food.name: Asado paraguayo
food.desc: Beef ribs, vacio and sausage grilled slowly over wood coals, served with cassava, sopa paraguaya and little else.

places.name: Parrillada Don Emilio
places.note: Locally famous for its asado; the reference grill in town.

places.name: Chipa Tia Churrasqueria
places.note: Buffet and grill combination that suits groups and big appetites.

places.name: El Quincho
places.note: Traditional grill plates with the full set of Paraguayan sides.

food.name: Surubi a la parrilla
food.desc: Giant Parana river catfish, firm and mild, grilled in thick steaks or stewed; the signature fish of the riverfront city.

places.name: La Cabana
places.note: Waterfront restaurant that specialises in surubi from the Parana.

places.name: Costanera restaurant strip
places.note: Row of river-view kitchens all serving surubi and other river fish.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Fish counters sell fresh surubi and nearby stalls will cook it simply.

food.name: Chipa guasu
food.desc: Baked pudding of fresh corn, cheese and onion, moister and sweeter than sopa paraguaya and served in the same way.

places.name: El Quincho
places.note: Reliable for the whole Paraguayan corn-and-cheese repertoire.

places.name: Taberna La Cava
places.note: Typical dishes at modest prices, chipa guasu included when in season.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Home cooks sell trays of it by weight most mornings.

food.name: Terere
food.desc: Yerba mate drunk ice cold with crushed medicinal herbs, shared from a guampa through a metal straw; Paraguay's national habit.

places.name: Costanera San Jose
places.note: The riverside promenade is where locals sit and pass the guampa all afternoon.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Yuyeras crush the herbs to order so you can build your own mix.

places.name: Plaza de Armas
places.note: Shaded benches and kiosks selling ice, yerba and herbs on the spot.

food.name: Mosto helado
food.desc: Chilled fresh sugarcane juice, sometimes with lemon, pressed at street carts and drunk in the summer heat.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Cane presses run through the morning; ask for it with lemon.

places.name: Costanera kiosks
places.note: Carts along the beach promenade sell it cold by the glass.

places.name: Circuito Comercial
places.note: Shopping streets near the border crossing are lined with juice carts.

landmarks: Jesuit Mission of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná
Paraguay's grandest UNESCO-listed Jesuit ruin, a vast 18th-century red-stone mission complex of carved friezes, cloisters and a monumental church.
Jesuit Mission of Jesús de Tavarangue
The hauntingly unfinished sister mission to Trinidad, its Moorish-arched church abandoned mid-construction when the Jesuits were expelled in 1767.
Costanera de Encarnación and Playa San José
A palm-lined riverfront promenade and urban beach on the Rio Paraná that turns the city into Paraguay's summer capital.
Sambodromo de Encarnación
The purpose-built parade avenue that hosts Paraguay's most famous Carnival, an explosion of feathers, floats and drumlines every summer weekend.
Catedral Nuestra Señora de la Encarnación
The city's stately hilltop cathedral, whose twin-towered facade presides over the central plaza and the faithful of southern Paraguay.
Plaza de Armas
Encarnación's leafy main square, a gathering place of fountains, monuments and craft vendors at the heart of the old commercial district.
San Roque González de Santa Cruz Bridge
The elegant cable-stayed international bridge spanning the Paraná to Posadas, Argentina, a symbol of the two riverside cities' intertwined lives.
Playa Mboi Ka'e
A quieter sandy river beach north of the center, favored by locals for sunset swims and views across the wide Paraná.
Antigua Estación del Ferrocarril
The restored 19th-century railway station, a nostalgic brick landmark recalling the steam-train era that first linked Encarnación to Asunción.
Jesuit Mission of San Cosme y Damián
A still-active mission village and colonial astronomy center, where restored Jesuit buildings house a planetarium honoring Father Buenaventura Suárez.

intl.to: Posadas (Argentina) - crosses the Paraná on the San Roque González de Santa Cruz bridge, ~15 min
intl.op: Tren Internacional Encarnación-Posadas — tickets at the station

train.note: Encarnacion has Paraguay's only passenger train and one of the shortest international rail services anywhere: a shuttle across the Parana to Posadas in Argentina alongside the San Roque Gonzalez de Santa Cruz bridge, taking about fifteen minutes, with immigration formalities handled in the terminals at each end. It runs a limited number of round trips a day from the modern terminal near the costanera, tickets are bought at the window for a few thousand guaranies, and the timetable is short and changes - check locally, as the service has been suspended for spells. Paraguay's national network, the old wood-burning Ferrocarril Carlos Antonio Lopez, has carried no scheduled domestic passengers since 2000, so there is no train to Asuncion or Ciudad del Este.

intl.to: Posadas (Argentina) - cross-border city buses over the international bridge
intl.op: Encarnación-Posadas international city bus operators — tickets on board

bus.note: The Terminal de Omnibus on Avenida Doctor Francia, about a kilometre north of the centre, handles everything from the frequent cross-border city buses to Posadas - roughly 30-40 minutes including the stops where you get off to have your passport stamped, and you must collect both the Paraguayan exit and Argentine entry stamps - to overnight coaches for Asuncion (5-6 hours) and Ciudad del Este (about 5). Crucero del Norte and other Argentine carriers sell long-haul tickets to Buenos Aires, and Paraguayan lines such as Nuestra Senora de la Asuncion work the domestic routes; tickets are sold at counters inside the terminal, cash or card. Buses will wait at the border posts if you tell the driver you need a stamp, but not indefinitely.

ferry.note: The old launch across the Parana between Encarnacion and Posadas stopped once the road-and-rail bridge opened, and the historic riverfront was flooded by the Yacyreta dam, so the waterfront is now a beach promenade rather than a port. There are no scheduled passenger boats; the river is used by barge traffic and by local fishing craft only.

half.name: San Ignacio Miní
half.blurb: Best-preserved Jesuit mission ruins in the region, across the border near Posadas, with red sandstone walls and carved facades.

half.name: Santa Ana Jesuit Ruins
half.blurb: Overgrown Jesuit mission ruins near San Ignacio, less restored and less visited, sitting quietly among jungle vegetation.
